chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: Screens and grit removal are widely employed in WWTPs as they enhance the operation and maintenance of subsequent treatment units. Recent innovations in pretreatment technologies have brought the heavy cost of grit in WWTPs operations lower which has been considered an unavoidable burden. For example, based on advanced Grit Management™, Headcell® grit separation system was developed to achieve optimum grit removal for more than 30 years in the UK and USA. Headcell® is capable of achieving 95% removal of all grit 75 μm and larger. Because of its no-moving part design involving a hydraulically driven system, it delivers grit removal over a wide range of flows in a much smaller energy footprint than the conventional removal systems (Barter and Sherony, 2011) . Table 5 lists several such advanced technologies currently being considered for pilot, demonstration, and full-scale operations in the North America.

chunks.text: However, these processes are costly, require high energy consumption and generally produce secondary waste which cannot remove the pollutants completely and then puts more pressure on the environment (Ghafari et al., 2008; Kapoor and Viraraghavan, 1997) . In contrast, biological treatment is generally regarded as a better choice for nitrate removal from wastewater due to its advantages of complete contaminants removal, economical and energy-saving. Currently, the complete denitrification process is widely applied for nitrate-containing wastewater treatment (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) . However, the traditional complete denitrification process (Eqs. ( 1 ) and ( 2 )) still presents some shortcomings, including high operational costs due to external organic carbon source requirements (Gu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2020) , large amounts of sludge yields and inevitable greenhouse gas emission, etc. (Du et al., 2016b) . Partial denitrification (PD) refers to the process of controlling NO 3 − -N reduced to NO 2 − -N without further reducing to nitrogen gas (N 2 ).

chunks.text: Presently, there are approximately 21,600 municipal wastewater treatment facilities serving 226.4 million people (USEPA, 2008) in the U.S. A large amount of biosolids including sludge and scum from these facilities are generated and then disposed either in landfills (28%) or in farmlands (45%, Willis et al., 2012) . This biosolid management practice has caused many environmental pollution and economic stress because biosolids landfilling raises disposal fee for the wastewater treatment facilities and releases methane as a strong greenhouse gas in landfills. Current research shows those biosolid wastes contain a good deal of energy. For example, the sludge collected from the primary and secondary treatment processes contains the energy of 8000 Btu per dry pound and scum contains 11,400 Btu per dry pound (Outwater, 1994; McCarty et al., 2011) . By recovering, utilizing, or selling the energy contained in those wastes, wastewater treatment facilities can reduce not only a large amount of waste disposal to landfills, eliminate the operation cost associated with the old practice, but generate extra revenue for better economic and societal benefit.

chunks.text: The SWTP with a treatment capacity of 120 million litres per day (MLD) treats municipal wastewater of the City of Saskatoon to create environmentally safe effluent before discharging into the South Saskatchewan River. It is an advanced class IV facility with a variety of technologies and processes including a grit and screen chamber, clarifiers, fermenters, dissolved air flotation (DAF) thickener, BNR using anaerobic, anoxic, and aerobic processes, ultraviolet disinfection system, nutrient recovery facility, anaerobic digesters, and biosolids facility (Fig. S2 ). Seasonal ambient temperatures typically vary between 30 °C and −40 °C and impact wastewater temperatures with averages of about 17 °C in summer and 13 °C in winter. The BNR processes and clarifiers are open-to-air treatment processes and sources of GHG and other gas emissions into the atmosphere. The study of SWTP GHG emissions from clarifiers and bioreactor processes and their operating parameters indicated that the aerobic reactor was the principal source of GHG emissions (Asadi and McPhedran, 2021a) .

chunks.text: The most commonly used advanced final treatment stage technologies were selected for our study. The tertiary treatments included different filtering (sand and cloth) and flotation techniques. Also, membrane bioreactor was selected. Micro-screen filtration with discfilters (DF) was examined in Viikinm€ aki WWTP located at Helsinki, a metropolitan area of Finland. Viikinm€ aki WWTP process is based on primary clarification, conventional activated sludge (CAS) process and a tertiary denitrifying biological filter (BAF). More detailed characteristics of each WWTPs included in this study is given in supplementary data (SD. Table S1 ). The pilot-scale discfilter (Hydrotech HSF 1702 -1F) consists of two discs composing each of 24 filter panels. The pilot unit was so-called inside-out system where the influent water is introduced inside the filter panels. The particle removal is based on physical retention in filters and sludge cake formation inside the filter panels. The sludge cake formation decelerates the filtering, causing water level rise inside the cylinder. When water meets the level sensor, backwash is initiated. Backwash is performed with high pressure (in this case 8 bars) to rinse off the sludge cake.

chunks.text: The wastewater treatment plant is designed with a processing capacity of 800 million litres/day of wastewater. Batten et al. [23] developed modified Melbourne's municipal wastewater treatment plant having a capacity of 770Ml/day, which was the basis of design of the process. The process of wastewater treatment adopted in this work is shown in Fig. 2 . The wastewater is assumed to be not severe polluted. The details of its composition can be found in the literature [17] . The initial step in the treatment of wastewater is the subtraction and removal of primary sludge. SiO 2 is considered as a model component for the wastewater grit. The present design considers a classifier for the grit removal unit operation which operates based on the difference in density [24] . In the literature, the primary treatment can reduce the Total Suspended Solids (TSS) by 50-60% [24] . Also, it implies the removal of the biological oxygen demand (BOD) in the incoming wastewater by 20-30%. Thus, the percentage of sludge removal by the primary treatment in the present model is chosen as 55%. An activated sludge process as the secondary treatment system for the effluent from the primary treatment is used in the present design.

chunks.text: Biological denitrification, i.e., the process of nitrate being reduced to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) by denitrifying bacteria, is an effective method to remove nitrogen from wastewater and has been widely applied in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) globally. However, the process requires a certain amount of carbon source as electron donors. Furthermore, the amount of organic matters in wastewater is always not enough to meet the demand of denitrifying bacteria because of the low carbon/nitrogen (C/N) ratio and the increasingly stringent discharge standards for total nitrogen (Zhang et al., 2016) . Thus, methanol, acetic acid, or similar organic matters are added as external carbon sources to enhance denitrification, which increases the operation costs (Latker et al., 2011) . As a by-product of wastewater treatment, waste activated sludge (WAS) contains a large amount of organic matter, that is a potential carbon source for denitrification (Zhang et al., 2009) .
